title: Given a set of distinct elements, generate all possible orderings (permutations) using backtracking.
shortTitle: Generate All Permutations of a Set (Backtracking)
keyPoints: A permutation uses all n elements in a specific order; n distinct elements have n! permutations
At each position try every unused element, mark it used, recurse, then unmark it (backtrack)
Record only at leaves when the path length equals n, unlike subsets which record at every node
A boolean used-array parallel to the input tracks which elements are in the current arrangement
The in-place swap variant permutes the array directly without a used-array, saving auxiliary space
For inputs with duplicates, sort and skip a candidate equal to its predecessor when the predecessor is unused
Time is O(n * n!) because n! permutations are each copied in O(n)

s1_definition.oneliner: Fill each position with every unused element, recurse, then undo, producing all n! orderings.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Permutation** – an arrangement of all elements of a set in a specific order. Order matters.
- **Count** – n distinct elements have n! (n factorial) permutations.
- **Used-marker** – a boolean array tracks which elements are in the current arrangement to prevent repetition within a single permutation.
- **Recording** – only at leaves (when path length equals n), because a permutation must use all elements.
- **Swap variant** – permutes the array in place without a used-array by swapping elements into the current position.
- **Complexity** – O(n * n!) time and space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India must try every possible processing order of a small batch of urgent transfers to find the sequence that best satisfies liquidity rules. A clerk fills a row of slots, one per transfer. In each slot she tries each remaining transfer, then moves to the next slot, systematically producing every ordering without repeating a transfer within one arrangement.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Permutations: [1, 2, 3]

  backtrack(path=[], used=[F,F,F])
  ├── pick 1 → backtrack([1], [T,F,F])
  │   ├── pick 2 → backtrack([1,2], [T,T,F])
  │   │   └── pick 3 → [1,2,3] ✓
  │   └── pick 3 → backtrack([1,3], [T,F,T])
  │       └── pick 2 → [1,3,2] ✓
  ├── pick 2 → backtrack([2], [F,T,F])
  │   ├── pick 1 → [2,1,3] ✓
  │   └── pick 3 → [2,3,1] ✓
  └── pick 3 → backtrack([3], [F,F,T])
      ├── pick 1 → [3,1,2] ✓
      └── pick 2 → [3,2,1] ✓

  Total: 3! = 6 permutations
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A permutation is an arrangement of all elements in a specific order, and n distinct elements have n! permutations. Backtracking generates them by filling one position at a time. At each position you try every unused element, mark it used, recurse to fill the next position, then unmark and remove.

The key differences from subsets are that order matters, all elements must be used, and you record only at leaves when the path is full. A boolean used-array parallel to the input prevents repeating an element within a single arrangement, and the add-mark-recurse-unmark-remove rhythm is the backtracking heartbeat.

For inputs with duplicates, sort first and skip a candidate equal to its predecessor when the predecessor is unused. The swap variant permutes the array in place without a used-array, saving auxiliary space. Both are valid interview answers.

At the National Bank of India, treasury used this to evaluate every processing order of a small batch of urgent transfers, finding the sequence that kept intraday liquidity within limits. The factorial growth means this is only feasible for small n, which is a key point to state.

Remember one sentence: try every unused element at each position, mark and unmark, and record only at full-length leaves.
